title: National and Regional Parties

cards.h: India's party system keeps changing shape
cards.b:
The party system is a favourite in Paper I. It is asked as a question on trends: from Congress dominance to coalitions to the BJP's rise, and on regional parties.

A party system is the pattern of competition among parties: how many matter, how strong they are and how they relate. Political scientists use it to describe stability and change.

India is unusual. It has a first-past-the-post system, which Duverger said favours two parties. Yet it has had one dominant party, a multi-party coalition era and, since 2014, a new dominant party with strong regional rivals.

This lesson gives you the phases, the key scholars and the facts on recognition of parties. The next lessons cover coalitions, pressure groups and voting behaviour.

cards.h: Four phases of the party system
cards.b: These phases follow the framework of Yogendra Yadav and Suhas Palshikar, who split the party system into stages: a Congress-dominant period; a period of challenge after 1967; a competitive multi-party period after 1989; and a new phase after 2014, which Palshikar called India's second dominant party system.

cards.h: Kothari and Morris-Jones on the Congress system
cards.b:
Rajni Kothari, "The Congress System in India" (1964)

In the 1950s and 60s the Congress was both government and a wide umbrella. It held within it many factions that bargained among themselves. Opposition parties were "parties of pressure" that influenced the Congress from outside. Competition took place within the dominant party. Congress was the "party of consensus"; the rest were "parties of pressure".

W.H. Morris-Jones

Described the system as one dominant party with several opposition parties of different kinds. Opposition's role was limited but real.

Why Congress dominated: it led the freedom movement, had a national organisation, social coalitions of upper castes, Dalits and Muslims, and the first-past-the-post system, which converted 45% of votes into about 75% of seats.

Why it broke: the 1967 election (Congress lost power in many states), the 1969 split, and later the Emergency (1975-77), after which the Janata Party won in 1977.

cards.h: Duverger's law and the Indian puzzle
cards.b:
Maurice Duverger, in Political Parties (1951), said that a plurality (first-past-the-post) system tends to produce two parties. India has many more.

Why? Pradeep Chhibber and Ken Kollman, in The Formation of National Party Systems (2004), argued that Duverger's effect works at the constituency and state level, where usually two or three parties compete. But the national system has many parties because the number of states with a strong regional party varies. As power moved to the states, parties became more regional.

So the national picture is a collection of different state-level contests: Congress-BJP in Gujarat and Rajasthan, DMK-AIADMK in Tamil Nadu, BJP-SP in Uttar Pradesh, and so on.

Other reasons for multi-party politics: caste and linguistic diversity, a federal structure, and the end of one party's national hold.

cards.h: How the ECI recognises national and state parties
cards.b:
The Election Commission recognises parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968. It reviews them after each general election. Recognised parties get a reserved symbol, free airtime on public media and electoral roll copies.

National party: (a) it wins 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11) from at least three states; or (b) it secures at least 6% of votes in four states and wins four Lok Sabha seats; or (c) it is recognised as a state party in four states.

State party (some tests): 6% of votes in the state and two assembly seats; or 3% of seats or three seats, whichever is higher; or 8% of votes.

On 10 April 2023, the ECI withdrew national status from the TMC, NCP and CPI and gave it to the AAP. The six national parties then were BJP, Congress, BSP, CPI(M), NPP and AAP. I found no report of a later change.

• Language and identity: the DMK (1949, C.N. Annadurai) and the Akali Dal (founded 1920).
  • Regional pride: the Telugu Desam (1982, N.T. Rama Rao) and the Asom Gana Parishad (1985).
  • Social justice and Mandal: the SP, RJD and BSP built on OBC and Dalit voters after 1989.
  • Congress decline: the vacuum was filled by locals. After 1967, many states went to non-Congress parties.
  • Splits from national parties: TMC (1998), NCP (1999), YSR Congress (2011), BJD (1997).
  • Economic reforms and federal bargaining: after 1991, states competed for investment and regional parties dealt with the Centre.

Regional parties became kingmakers in coalition governments from 1996 to 2014. In 2024, the TDP and JD(U) helped the NDA reach a majority.

cards.h: Strengths and weaknesses of this pattern
cards.b:
Strengths:

  • Regional parties give voice to local identities and make a diverse country feel represented.
  • They keep the Centre accountable; the NDA and UPA both needed their consent.
  • They push states' interests on finance, language and water.

Criticisms:

  • Personality and dynasty: Kanchan Chandra's Democratic Dynasties (2016) shows that where parties lack institutions, family succession becomes common.
  • Oligarchy: Robert Michels's "iron law of oligarchy" in Political Parties (1911) applies, with little intra-party democracy.
  • Pragmatic alliances weaken ideology; leaders switch sides.
  • Regionalism can obstruct national policy, such as river or Centre-state fiscal talks.
  • Money and criminalisation (see lesson on electoral behaviour).

cards.h: The BJP era and the shape of competition
cards.b:
Scholars such as Suhas Palshikar note that BJP dominance after 2014 differs from Congress dominance. It rests on a strong organisation, a leader with a direct link to voters and a Hindutva-plus-welfare appeal, yet it faces strong rival parties in many states. It did not erase regional politics, and its dominance is uneven.

Key moments:

  • 2014: BJP won 282 seats, the first single-party majority since 1984.
  • 2019: BJP 303.
  • 2024: BJP 240 and NDA 293; Congress 99. The BJP fell short of 272 and relied on allies, so the coalition feature returned.

Other trends: a rise in welfare politics (direct benefit transfer), and growth of "third force" parties that are neither Congress nor BJP in the states.

• Lok Sabha 2024: BJP 240, Congress 99, SP 37, TMC 29, DMK 22, TDP 16, JD(U) 12. NDA 293 against the INDIA bloc's 234.
  • Delhi 2025: BJP defeated the AAP, ending its decade in power.
  • Bihar, November 2025: the NDA won 202 of 243 seats, with BJP 89 and JD(U) 85. The Mahagathbandhan was reduced to the mid-thirties.
  • May 2026: reports show the BJP winning West Bengal for the first time, the Congress-led UDF returning in Kerala, and Vijay's new party TVK emerging as the largest party in Tamil Nadu, ending the DMK government. Check the final results and ministries before using exact seat numbers.

Lesson for answers: the national picture is the sum of different state contests, and incumbency and welfare matter more than ever.

Structure: define party system; Kothari and Morris-Jones for the first phase; the 1967 shock; coalition era after 1989; Chhibber-Kollman on why Duverger fails nationally; 2014 and 2024 results; regional party roles and flaws; ECI recognition rules; balanced conclusion.
